meta.blurb: For three years Watson believed his friend was dead. Then an old book collector turns up in his study and takes off his disguise. Thirteen cases follow, with dancing men, six plaster Napoleons and a blackmailer in a fine house.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the consulting detective of Baker Street, calm, quick and proud; believed dead after the Reichenbach Falls in 1891 and back in 1894. Dr Watson: his friend and the narrator, a doctor. Mrs Hudson: the landlady. Inspector Lestrade and Inspector Stanley Hopkins: Scotland Yard detectives. Baker Street, London. The thirteen stories in order: The Empty House; The Norwood Builder; The Dancing Men; The Solitary Cyclist; The Priory School; Black Peter; Charles Augustus Milverton; The Six Napoleons; The Three Students; The Golden Pince-Nez; The Missing Three-Quarter; The Abbey Grange; The Second Stain. The Empty House: the Honourable Ronald Adair, shot dead in a locked room at Park Lane; Colonel Sebastian Moran, the right hand of the late Professor Moriarty, who fires an air gun; a wax bust of Holmes; the Reichenbach Falls; Mycroft Holmes. The Norwood Builder: John Hector McFarlane, a young solicitor; Jonas Oldacre, a builder, who fakes his own death; Deep Dene House, Norwood. The Dancing Men: Hilton Cubitt of Ridling Thorpe Manor, Norfolk; his wife Elsie, an American; Abe Slaney of Chicago; Inspector Martin. The Solitary Cyclist: Violet Smith, a music teacher; Mr Woodley; a drunken clergyman; Charlington; South Africa. The Priory School: Dr Thorneycroft Huxtable; Lord Saltire, aged ten; the Duke of Holdernesse; Herr Heidegger, the German master; James Wilder, the Duke's secretary; Reuben Hayes of the Fighting Cock inn. Black Peter: Captain Peter Carey, called Black Peter; Woodman's Lee, Sussex; Patrick Cairns, a harpooner; John Hopley Neligan; the ship Sea Unicorn. Charles Augustus Milverton: the blackmailer of Appledore Towers, Hampstead; Lady Eva Blackwell; the Earl of Dovercourt. The Six Napoleons: Lestrade; the black pearl of the Borgias; the Prince of Colonna; Beppo; Mr Josiah Brown of Chiswick; Harding Brothers. The Three Students: Hilton Soames, a tutor at St Luke's College; Bannister, the servant; Gilchrist, an athlete; Daulat Ras; Miles McLaren; Thucydides. The Golden Pince-Nez: Professor Coram; Willoughby Smith, his secretary; Yoxley Old Place; Russia. The Missing Three-Quarter: Cyril Overton, captain of the Cambridge rugby team; Godfrey Staunton; Dr Leslie Armstrong; Lord Mount-James; Pompey, the hound; Oxford, Cambridge. The Abbey Grange: Sir Eustace Brackenstall; Lady Brackenstall; Captain Jack Croker; Theresa Wright, the maid; Kent; the Randall gang; Australia. The Second Stain: Lord Bellinger, the Prime Minister; the Right Honourable Trelawney Hope, European Secretary; Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope; Eduardo Lucas, a spy; Godolphin Street. Voice and tone: lively, clear and clever, each case a small, complete puzzle; deaths are stated plainly and without gore. Beat 50 closes the whole book.

beats.scene: A tall house in Park Lane stands under a grey London sky
beats.summary: The Empty House: In 1894 the Honourable Ronald Adair is shot dead in a locked room, and Watson goes to see the house.

beats.scene: An old book collector drops his books at the feet of a startled Watson
beats.summary: An old book collector bumps into Watson, then appears in his study and is revealed as Holmes.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson sit together by the fire, one pale and one amazed
beats.summary: Holmes explains that he survived the Reichenbach Falls by a wrestling trick, and has been abroad for three years.

beats.scene: A wax bust of Holmes sits in a lit window of Baker Street
beats.summary: At night Holmes and Watson wait in an empty house opposite Baker Street, where a wax figure sits in Holmes's window.

beats.scene: A heavy man raises an air gun at a dark window
beats.summary: Colonel Moran fires at the wax figure and is arrested; he had shot Adair, who caught him cheating at cards.

beats.scene: A pale young lawyer rushes into Holmes's room with a newspaper
beats.summary: The Norwood Builder: a young solicitor, McFarlane, says he is about to be arrested for the murder of a builder.

beats.scene: Lestrade points to a bloody thumb mark on a hall wall
beats.summary: Lestrade arrests McFarlane; Holmes says the bloody thumb mark was not there the day before.

beats.scene: Holmes lights a small fire of straw in a wooden hall
beats.summary: Holmes finds a hidden space in the house and lights a smoky fire to bring out whoever hides in it.

beats.scene: A little round man bursts out of a hidden door, coughing in the smoke
beats.summary: Oldacre comes out of his hiding place; he had wanted revenge on McFarlane's mother and faked his own death.

beats.scene: A country gentleman lays a sheet of little dancing figures on a table
beats.summary: The Dancing Men: Hilton Cubitt shows Holmes strange drawings that have frightened his wife, Elsie.

beats.scene: Holmes sits among papers covered with rows of little dancing figures
beats.summary: Holmes sees that the drawings are a secret writing in which each figure is a letter.

beats.scene: Holmes reads a telegram beside a railway timetable with a pale face
beats.summary: Holmes decodes the last message, a threat to Elsie, and learns that the writer is Abe Slaney of Chicago.

beats.scene: A dark country house at dawn with servants standing at the door
beats.summary: At Ridling Thorpe Manor, Hilton Cubitt is found dead and Elsie is badly wounded.

beats.scene: A man in a garden reads a note of dancing figures as police wait
beats.summary: Holmes writes a dancing-men message to lure Slaney; the police arrest him and Elsie recovers.

beats.scene: A young woman on a lonely road looks back at a distant cyclist
beats.summary: The Solitary Cyclist: Violet Smith, a music teacher, is followed on a lonely road by a bearded cyclist.

beats.scene: Two men with coarse faces whisper at an inn table
beats.summary: Holmes learns that Violet will inherit money and that Woodley wants to marry her for it.

beats.scene: A pistol shot rings out in a room as a young woman is rescued
beats.summary: Woodley forces Violet into a wedding; the cyclist shoots him and Holmes arrives to see Violet safe.

beats.scene: A pale headmaster slumps on the carpet of Holmes's sitting room
beats.summary: The Priory School: Dr Huxtable collapses in Holmes's room and reports that the Duke's ten-year-old son has vanished.

beats.scene: Holmes kneels on the moor beside bicycle tracks and strange hoof prints
beats.summary: On the moor Holmes follows bicycle tracks and odd cow prints, and finds the German master dead.

beats.scene: A lonely country inn with a painted sign of a fighting cock
beats.summary: The false cow tracks lead Holmes to the Fighting Cock inn, where the missing boy is hidden.

beats.scene: Holmes speaks gravely to a proud old duke in a grand hall
beats.summary: Holmes tells the Duke that his secretary James Wilder, his secret son, planned the kidnapping.

beats.scene: A wooden hut stands alone in a garden beside an old house
beats.summary: Black Peter: a fierce whaling captain is found dead in his hut, killed with a harpoon, and Hopkins asks Holmes to come.

beats.scene: Holmes drives a harpoon into a dead pig in a butcher's shop
beats.summary: Holmes finds a tobacco pouch and a notebook with the letters J H N, and tests a harpoon on a dead pig.

beats.scene: Holmes snaps handcuffs onto a huge black-bearded sailor in his room
beats.summary: Holmes lures the killer, Patrick Cairns, with an advertisement and handcuffs him.

beats.scene: A smooth man sits behind a desk in a grand room, smiling coldly
beats.summary: Charles Augustus Milverton: Holmes meets the blackmailer Milverton, who wants seven thousand pounds for Lady Eva Blackwell's letters.

beats.scene: A rough young plumber with a pipe walks beside a housemaid
beats.summary: Holmes disguises himself as a plumber and becomes engaged to Milverton's housemaid to learn the house.

beats.scene: Two men hide behind a curtain as a veiled woman raises a revolver
beats.summary: Holmes and Watson break in at night; a veiled woman enters the study and shoots Milverton dead.

beats.scene: Papers burn in a fireplace while police whistles sound in the dark
beats.summary: Holmes burns the letters from Milverton's safe, and later refuses to help Lestrade catch the woman.

beats.scene: A man smashes a plaster bust of Napoleon on a dark London street
beats.summary: The Six Napoleons: Lestrade reports that someone is breaking plaster busts of Napoleon all over London.

beats.scene: A black pearl shines in a velvet box in a hotel room
beats.summary: Holmes recalls that the Borgia black pearl was stolen from a prince, and guesses it is hidden in one of the busts.

beats.scene: Three men wait in a dark garden behind a house in Chiswick
beats.summary: Holmes works out where the sixth bust stands and waits with Lestrade in a Chiswick garden.

beats.scene: Holmes holds up a bright black pearl above shattered white plaster
beats.summary: Beppo smashes the sixth bust and is caught; the pearl is found, and Lestrade applauds Holmes.

beats.scene: A worried tutor stands by a desk covered with printed pages
beats.summary: The Three Students: at St Luke's College, a tutor finds that someone has looked at the proofs of an exam.

beats.scene: Holmes studies a small black lump and pencil shavings on a desk
beats.summary: Holmes finds pencil shavings and black clay in the study and meets the three students.

beats.scene: A young athlete bows his head in front of Holmes and his tutor
beats.summary: Holmes shows that the clay came from Gilchrist's jumping shoes; Gilchrist confesses and gives up the scholarship.

beats.scene: A pair of gold glasses lies in the hand of a man outdoors
beats.summary: The Golden Pince-Nez: Hopkins brings Holmes the murder of Professor Coram's secretary, who held a pair of gold glasses.

beats.scene: Holmes holds up gold glasses to the light and describes their owner
beats.summary: From the glasses Holmes describes the owner, a short-sighted woman, and studies the professor's rooms.

beats.scene: A tall pale woman steps out of a hidden space in an old study
beats.summary: Holmes finds the woman, a Russian whose story of an old betrayal explains the crime.

beats.scene: A huge rugby captain stands in Holmes's doorway with a worried face
beats.summary: The Missing Three-Quarter: Cyril Overton asks Holmes to find his star player Godfrey Staunton, who vanished before the Oxford match.

beats.scene: A hound follows a scent along a country road beside a carriage
beats.summary: In Cambridge Holmes uses the hound Pompey to follow the scent of aniseed to a lonely cottage.

beats.scene: A young man weeps beside the bed of his sick wife in a cottage
beats.summary: Staunton is found with his dying young wife, whom he had married in secret.

beats.scene: A lady sits tied to a chair in a dining room beside a bell-rope
beats.summary: The Abbey Grange: Sir Eustace Brackenstall is found dead, and his wife says burglars tied her to a chair.

beats.scene: Holmes looks closely at a cut bell-rope and the knots on a chair
beats.summary: Holmes sees that the rope was cut, not torn, that the knots are a sailor's, and that the burglars' story is false.

beats.scene: A young sea captain stands in a quiet room, speaking honestly to Holmes
beats.summary: Holmes traces the clues to Captain Jack Croker, who loved Lady Brackenstall and confesses.

beats.scene: Holmes shakes the hand of a young sea captain as a lady watches
beats.summary: Holmes judges that Croker acted to save a woman and lets him go free.

beats.scene: Two grave statesmen sit in Holmes's sitting room at Baker Street
beats.summary: The Second Stain: the Prime Minister and the European Secretary ask Holmes to find a stolen letter that could cause a war.

beats.scene: A policeman stands at the door of a quiet house in Godolphin Street
beats.summary: Holmes suspects the spy Eduardo Lucas, but Lucas is found murdered in his house.

beats.scene: Holmes kneels on a carpet beside two dark stains
beats.summary: Holmes sees that the stain on the carpet does not lie over the stain on the floor, so the carpet was lifted.

beats.scene: Holmes lifts a loose board and takes out a folded letter
beats.summary: Holmes finds the letter hidden under the floor; Lady Hilda admits she took it to protect a secret.

beats.scene: Two statesmen stare in amazement at a letter inside an open box
beats.summary: Holmes shows that the letter is back in the despatch box and keeps Lady Hilda's secret; the book ends.

B1B2: In The Empty House, a young gentleman named Ronald Adair is found shot dead in a locked room in London. Dr Watson, who has been without his friend Holmes for three years, goes to look at the house.

While Watson stands looking at the house, an old book collector bumps into him and drops his books. Later the same old man visits Watson's rooms, takes off his disguise, and turns out to be Sherlock Holmes.

Holmes explains that he used a clever wrestling trick at the Reichenbach Falls, so that only Moriarty fell. He then stayed hidden abroad for three years, because Moriarty's friends were still hunting him.
That night Holmes leads Watson into an empty house opposite his old rooms in Baker Street. In the window of his rooms sits a wax bust of Holmes, which Mrs Hudson moves from time to time.

At last a man creeps into the empty house with a strange air gun and shoots at the wax figure. Holmes seizes him, and Inspector Lestrade arrives to arrest Colonel Sebastian Moran for the murder of Adair.

In The Norwood Builder, a young lawyer named McFarlane rushes into Baker Street and says he will soon be arrested for murder. A builder called Jonas Oldacre has vanished, and McFarlane's walking stick is stained with blood.
Lestrade arrests McFarlane and proudly shows Holmes a bloody thumb mark on the hall wall. Holmes studies it for a long time and says, with a strange smile, that it was not there the day before.
Holmes measures the house and finds a hidden space behind the walls, so he lights a small fire of straw and wet wood. When the smoke rolls through the hall, Holmes shouts that the house is on fire.
The smoke drives a man out of his hiding place, coughing and angry. It is Jonas Oldacre himself, alive and well, and he planned to blame McFarlane for a murder that never happened.
In The Dancing Men, Hilton Cubitt, a Norfolk gentleman, shows Holmes a row of drawings of little dancing figures. They have appeared at his house, and his wife, Elsie, is terrified by them.

Holmes studies the copies carefully and decides that the little men are a kind of secret writing. Each figure, he believes, stands for one letter, and the figures that carry flags mark the end of a word.
When Holmes breaks the code, the last message reads, “Elsie, prepare to meet thy God.” He learns that the writer is Abe Slaney, a dangerous man from Chicago, and he hurries by train to Norfolk.
At Ridling Thorpe Manor, Holmes and Watson find that they have come too late. Hilton Cubitt has been shot dead in his room, and Elsie lies unconscious beside him with a terrible wound.

Holmes writes a note in the dancing men code that tells Slaney to come at once, and the criminal walks into the trap. Inspector Martin arrests him, and Elsie, to everyone's relief, slowly recovers from her wound.
In The Solitary Cyclist, a young music teacher named Violet Smith tells Holmes that a bearded man on a bicycle follows her. He never speaks to her, and he rides away whenever she tries to approach.
Holmes learns that Violet is the heir of an uncle who died rich in South Africa. Mr Woodley, a coarse and violent man, wants to marry her for her money, and he has hired a drunken clergyman.
Woodley and the drunken clergyman try to force Violet into a wedding in a lonely place. The solitary cyclist bursts in and wounds Woodley with a pistol, and Holmes arrives in time to see Violet safe.

In The Priory School, a famous headmaster, Dr Huxtable, collapses on Holmes's floor and then tells his tale. The ten-year-old son of the Duke of Holdernesse has vanished from his school, along with a German teacher.
On the moor, Holmes follows the tracks of a bicycle and then a line of cow prints that do not look right to him. He soon finds the German master dead on the moor, and Lord Saltire is still missing.
The strange tracks lead Holmes to the Fighting Cock inn, whose owner, Reuben Hayes, keeps horses with cow-shaped shoes. In a back room of the inn, the missing boy is found alive and well.
Holmes goes to the Duke and tells him that his secretary, James Wilder, is behind the kidnapping. Wilder is the Duke's secret son, and he hated the boy who would inherit everything.

In Black Peter, a bad-tempered whaling captain named Peter Carey is found dead in a wooden hut near his house in Sussex. A harpoon has been driven right through him, and Inspector Hopkins asks Holmes to come.
In the hut, Holmes finds a tobacco pouch that is not Carey's, and a notebook with the letters J H N. He also drives a harpoon into a dead pig, to learn how strong the killer must have been.

Holmes places an advertisement for a harpooner for the ship Sea Unicorn, and several men come to answer it. The last of them is Patrick Cairns, a huge sailor, and Holmes handcuffs him as soon as he enters.

In Charles Augustus Milverton, Holmes meets the worst man in London, a blackmailer who keeps ladies' letters. Milverton refuses to sell Lady Eva Blackwell's letters for less than seven thousand pounds.
Holmes finds that open argument is useless, so he plans to take the letters by stealth. Disguised as a plumber, he courts Milverton's housemaid and learns the plan of the house.
That night Holmes and Watson break into Appledore Towers and hide behind a curtain in Milverton's study. A veiled woman arrives, speaks to Milverton, and then shoots him dead.

Holmes and Watson burn all the letters in Milverton's safe, and then escape over the garden wall. When Lestrade asks Holmes to help catch the killer, Holmes refuses, because he feels that Milverton deserved his fate.

In The Six Napoleons, Lestrade visits Baker Street to tell Holmes about a very strange series of crimes. Someone is breaking into houses and shops, and all he takes is a plaster bust of Napoleon, which he smashes in the street.
Holmes learns that the Black Pearl of the Borgias was stolen from a prince's hotel room. He soon guesses that the thief has hidden the pearl inside a plaster bust, and now he must find which one.
Holmes learns that the last bust stands in the house of Mr Josiah Brown in Chiswick. That night he, Watson and Lestrade wait in the dark garden for the man who breaks busts.
A man climbs through the window, takes the last bust to the garden and smashes it. Holmes and Lestrade seize him, and Holmes holds up the lost pearl, shining in the broken plaster.
In The Three Students, a tutor named Hilton Soames finds that someone has looked at the examination papers on his desk. Three students live on the floor above, and any of them might be the cheat.
In the study Holmes finds some curls of pencil wood and a small lump of black clay. He then meets the three students, Gilchrist, Daulat Ras and Miles McLaren, in their rooms.

Holmes shows that the clay on the desk came from Gilchrist's jumping shoes, and the young athlete confesses at once. Ashamed of his weakness, he gives up the scholarship and promises to start a new life abroad.
In The Golden Pince-Nez, Inspector Hopkins tells Holmes that Professor Coram's secretary, Willoughby Smith, has been found dead. In the dying man's hand was a pair of gold glasses.

Holmes studies the pince-nez and describes their owner in detail: a woman with a narrow nose, close eyes and very weak sight. At Yoxley Old Place he notices that the professor's bedroom leads off the study, and that a person could hide there.
Holmes opens a hidden space in the professor's rooms and finds the woman who has been hiding there. She is Russian, and her story of an old betrayal explains why the secretary died.

In The Missing Three-Quarter, a huge rugby captain named Cyril Overton begs Holmes to find a player who has vanished. Godfrey Staunton, the team's best three-quarter, left his hotel after a strange message, and the Oxford match is tomorrow.

In Cambridge, Dr Leslie Armstrong refuses to answer Holmes's questions, so Holmes uses a dog named Pompey. The dog follows the smell of aniseed along a country road, and it leads them to a small cottage.
In the cottage Staunton sits by the bed of his wife, whom he had married in secret. She is dying of a lung illness, and he dared not tell his rich, mean uncle, Lord Mount-James.

In The Abbey Grange, Inspector Hopkins takes Holmes to a country house in Kent where Sir Eustace Brackenstall has been found dead. His wife, Lady Brackenstall, says that three burglars tied her to a chair and killed her husband.
Holmes sees that the bell-rope was cut, not torn down, and that the knots on the chair are a sailor's knots. He decides that the story of the Randall gang is false, and that a seaman may be involved.

Holmes follows the clues to a sea captain named Jack Croker, who had been Lady Brackenstall's friend before her marriage. Croker admits that he came to the house, and that he and the lady had lied to the police.
Holmes listens to the whole story and says that he will be judge in his own court of law. Believing that Croker saved a woman from a cruel man, he lets the captain walk free.
In The Second Stain, the Prime Minister and the European Secretary visit Holmes in secret. A letter from a foreign ruler has vanished from a locked box, and if it becomes public, it could mean war.

Holmes suspects that the spy Eduardo Lucas has the letter, but the next morning Lucas is found murdered in his house. Inspector Lestrade is in charge, and a large bloodstain has soaked through the carpet of the room.

In the room where Lucas died, Holmes notices that the bloodstain on the carpet does not lie above the stain on the floor. He realises that someone has lifted the carpet, and he guesses that it was done to reach a hiding place.
Holmes lifts a board in the floor and finds the missing letter hidden in a hollow beneath it. He then visits Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, who admits that she took it to protect a secret from her past.

When the Prime Minister and Mr Hope return to Baker Street, Holmes asks Hope to open his despatch box again. Inside, to everyone's amazement, lies the letter, and Holmes calmly refuses to say how it got there.
C1C2: In the spring of 1894, the whole of London was shaken by the murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair, a gentle, popular young man who was found shot dead in a locked room of his mother's house in Park Lane. Nobody could explain how a murderer had entered the room, or how he had left it again, and the police had no theory to offer. Dr Watson, who had been without his friend Sherlock Holmes for three years, found that the mystery drew him irresistibly to Park Lane.

As Watson stood outside the house, a bent old man with a pile of books under his arm jostled him roughly, and a short while later the same man appeared in Watson's own study to offer an apology. The old man pulled off his white hair and his false whiskers, and there, smiling, stood Sherlock Holmes, whom the world had believed dead since the fall at the Reichenbach Falls. Watson, who had never fainted in his life, felt the room turn dark and slowly sank to the floor.

Holmes explained that his skill in a Japanese form of wrestling had saved him at the edge of the Reichenbach Falls, where he had slipped aside and let Professor Moriarty fall alone into the abyss. Fearing the revenge of the professor's gang, he had let the world believe him dead, and during three years of wandering he had visited Tibet, Persia and Khartoum, and had done some chemical research in the south of France. Only his brother Mycroft had known the truth, and now, with one of the gang's cleverest men still at large, he had hurried home.

That night Holmes led his friend through back streets and over a wall into an empty house exactly opposite the old rooms in Baker Street, where nothing had been changed. In the sitting-room window, lit from behind by a lamp, stood a wax figure of Holmes himself, which his landlady Mrs Hudson turned a little every quarter of an hour so that it should seem to be alive. Holmes whispered that he was waiting for a man who, he was sure, would soon try to shoot him.

At last a heavy-shouldered man slipped into the dark room beside them, raised a curious air gun to the window and fired at the wax head, which was struck by the bullet with a dull thud. Holmes sprang upon him, and within a minute Inspector Lestrade was arresting Colonel Sebastian Moran, once a distinguished soldier and the right hand of Professor Moriarty. It was Moran who had shot young Adair, who had caught him cheating at cards, and Holmes counted the capture as the proper end of his long fight with the professor's gang.

John Hector McFarlane, a young solicitor, burst into Baker Street with the news that the police were about to arrest him for the murder of Jonas Oldacre, a retired builder of Norwood. Oldacre had summoned him only the evening before and had astonished him by making a will in his favour, and during the night a great fire had burned in the builder's timber-yard, and the builder himself had vanished. Lestrade, with a bloodstained walking stick and a thumb mark on the wall of the hall, was convinced that the case was already complete.

Lestrade, delighted with his own cleverness, arrested McFarlane and took Holmes and Watson to Deep Dene House, where he proudly showed them a bloody thumb mark left upon the wall of the hall. Holmes examined it with his lens and agreed that it was McFarlane's own, yet he added, with a curious smile, that it had not been there when the hall was searched the day before. Lestrade laughed at the idea, though a small doubt crept for the first time into his triumphant mind.

Holmes walked slowly through the house with a measuring tape, and found that the upstairs rooms did not fit the plan of the rooms below, so that a space of some size must be hidden behind the walls. He ordered a small fire of straw and wet wood to be lit in the hall, and when the smoke began to curl into the corridors, he shouted a cry of fire that rang through the empty house. It was a cruel trick, perhaps, but it was also the only way to bring a hiding man out of his hole.

A little round man burst out of a hole in the wall, coughing and spluttering, and Holmes cheerfully introduced him to Lestrade as Mr Jonas Oldacre, very much alive. The builder had borne a grudge against McFarlane's mother, who had refused him many years before, and he had planned to take his revenge on the son by making him seem a murderer. The thumb mark, Holmes explained, had been taken from a wax seal on a letter, and Lestrade, with the grace of a beaten man, admitted that the great detective was right.

Hilton Cubitt, a tall and honest country gentleman from Norfolk, laid before Holmes a series of childish drawings of little dancing men, which had begun to appear on the doors and walls of his house. His wife Elsie, an American whom he had married a year before, had grown pale and fearful at the very sight of them, though she would say nothing, having made him promise never to ask about her past. He loved her too much to break his word, and so he had come to the one man who might read the strange pictures.

Holmes sat late over the copies, comparing the postures of the little figures until he was convinced that the drawings were a secret writing, in which every dancing man stood for a letter. The commonest figure, he reasoned, must be the letter E, which is the commonest in English, and the figures that carried small flags seemed to mark the ends of words. From these few clues, with the patience of a man doing a difficult sum, he began to build up the whole alphabet.

At last the code surrendered, and the final message in the series, once Holmes had read it, was a cruel threat: “Elsie, prepare to meet thy God.” A cable to America soon revealed that the writer was Abe Slaney, a dangerous criminal who had once known Elsie in Chicago, and Holmes, white with anxiety, hurried to Norfolk by the first train. He feared that the danger was no mere threat, and as the train rushed through the dark countryside, he sat silent, as if willing it to go faster.

The two men reached Ridling Thorpe Manor in the early morning, only to find the house in confusion and the servants weeping, for Hilton Cubitt lay dead upon the floor of his room with a bullet through his heart. His wife Elsie, who had been found beside him with a terrible wound, was carried upstairs to a bed, and the doctor feared the worst. Holmes bent over the room, noting the open window, the smell of powder and the second bullet that had missed its mark and struck the frame.

Holmes drew a few dancing men of his own, and the message, which in plain English was an urgent call to come at once, was placed where Slaney would see it. The American, who was sure that only Elsie could have sent such a note, walked boldly into the garden and into the arms of Inspector Martin, and he never learned who had tricked him. Elsie slowly recovered from her wound, and the court, in the end, decided that Slaney must answer for the death of her husband.

Violet Smith, a young woman of independent spirit who earned her living as a music teacher, came to Baker Street with a strange complaint. On the lonely road between the station and her employer's house, a bearded man on a bicycle followed her each week, and he never spoke a word. When she turned to confront him he sped away as though he feared her, and meanwhile a coarse and florid visitor named Woodley had begun to pay her unwelcome attention.

Holmes soon discovered that Violet's long-lost uncle had died in South Africa, a rich man, and that she was his only heir, a fact that she herself did not yet know. Mr Woodley, a coarse and violent man who had returned from the same country, meant to marry her for the money, and to that end had engaged a drunken, disgraced clergyman to perform the ceremony. Holmes understood that the solitary cyclist was no villain, and that the girl's real danger lay in the house to which she went each week.

Woodley and his drunken clergyman had seized Violet and were already forcing her through a wedding service when the solitary cyclist, who had followed them all the way, burst into the room with a pistol in his hand. He fired at Woodley and wounded him, and as the villain fell, Holmes and Watson arrived to find the clergyman cowering and Violet safe, though pale and shaken. The marriage, Holmes pointed out, was worth nothing in law, since she had never agreed to it, and the matter was soon in the hands of the police.

Dr Thorneycroft Huxtable, the famous headmaster of the Priory School, staggered into Holmes's room and sank down in a faint, and when he was revived, he told a story that shook London. Lord Saltire, the ten-year-old son and heir of the Duke of Holdernesse, had vanished from his bed in the night, and with him the German master, Herr Heidegger, who had left the school in a hurry. The Duke, who was among the greatest men in England, had offered a large reward, and Holmes, who liked both the money and the puzzle, agreed to go north at once.

On the great moor, Holmes found the track of a bicycle, which vanished into some boggy ground, and beyond it a line of cow prints that were not what they seemed. A short distance further on, the body of the unfortunate German master lay in a hollow, struck down by a heavy blow to the head. Of the boy there was no sign, and Holmes announced, to the headmaster's horror, that the affair was a good deal more serious than a simple kidnapping.

The false cow tracks led Holmes to the Fighting Cock, a lonely inn kept by a rough man named Reuben Hayes, in whose stable he found horses with shoes made to leave the print of a cow's hoof. A hidden room of the inn held the missing boy, safe though frightened, and Holmes understood that he had been taken by someone who knew the district well and who wished to be thought a stranger. The trail, as he told Watson with quiet satisfaction, now pointed straight to the Duke's own household.

Holmes put the whole matter before the Duke of Holdernesse in his great house, and he told him with grave courtesy that his own secretary, James Wilder, had planned the kidnapping. Wilder was the Duke's secret son, born before his marriage, and he had hated the lawful heir with a bitterness that grew with every year. The Duke, shamed and shaken, paid the promised reward, and Holmes, putting the cheque in his pocket, promised that the sad story should go no further than the room.

Captain Peter Carey, called Black Peter by the seamen who had served under him, was a fierce, drunken man whose temper was the terror of his family. He was found dead one morning in the wooden hut that he had built beside his house at Woodman's Lee in Sussex, pinned to the wall by a harpoon that had passed clean through his body. Young Inspector Stanley Hopkins, who admired Holmes as a pupil admires a master, asked him to come and look at the hut.

Inside the hut, Holmes found a sealskin tobacco pouch marked P C, which did not belong to the dead man, together with a notebook in which one set of initials, J H N, appeared again and again. To learn what strength the killer must have had, he went to a butcher's shop and drove a harpoon at a dead pig, an experiment that he cheerfully failed to repeat to his own satisfaction. A man who could do what had been done to Black Peter, he concluded, was a powerful sailor, and probably an experienced harpooner.

Holmes placed a notice in the newspapers asking for a skilled harpooner to join the ship Sea Unicorn, and before long three men appeared at Baker Street. The last to arrive was Patrick Cairns, a huge, black-bearded sailor, and Holmes locked handcuffs on his wrists with a single movement before he knew what had happened. Cairns confessed that he had killed Carey in a violent quarrel over money, and the young man whom the police had arrested by mistake, John Hopley Neligan, was cleared of all suspicion.

Charles Augustus Milverton, whom Holmes called the worst man in London, grew rich by buying the private letters of ladies and gentlemen and selling them back at a terrible price. Lady Eva Blackwell, a beautiful girl who was about to be married, had written some foolish letters in the past, and Milverton refused to let them go for less than seven thousand pounds, which she could never find. Holmes, who had met him in his own handsome house, left with a cold fury, for he saw that no law in England could reach the man.

Since law and persuasion were both useless, Holmes resolved on a daring plan, and he astonished Watson by revealing that he meant to break into Milverton's house and take the letters by force. For some days he lived the life of a plumber, a rough young man with a pipe and a cheap moustache, and he walked out with Milverton's housemaid, who told him a great deal about the house. He even became engaged to her, he said, with a regretful smile, and Watson was left to wonder what would become of the poor girl.

On the chosen night, Holmes and Watson crept through the conservatory into Appledore Towers, and in the quiet study they were just opening the safe when a sound in the passage made them dart behind a heavy curtain. Milverton came in, followed by a veiled woman who accused him in a low, shaking voice of having ruined her life, and before he could answer, she drew a revolver and shot him dead. She fled as quickly as she had come, leaving the two friends alone with the body.

When the woman had fled, Holmes calmly emptied the safe, and the letters of many frightened people were burned in the grate so that Milverton might never again threaten them. The two friends escaped over the garden wall, with police whistles shrilling behind them, and returned safely to Baker Street. When Lestrade came the next day to ask Holmes's help in tracing the murderer, the detective answered coolly that his sympathies were with the criminals, and that he would not take the case.

Lestrade, who rarely brought Holmes anything but cases that he could not understand, came one evening with a story that made even the detective smile. A man had broken into several houses and had taken nothing but a cheap plaster bust of Napoleon, which he smashed in the street, and a dead man had been found in one garden. Holmes, delighted by the absurdity of it, asked where the busts had come from, since a puzzle of this kind is rarely as foolish as it seems.

Holmes recalled that, only a few days earlier, the great black pearl of the Borgias had been stolen from the hotel room of the Prince of Colonna, and that one of the prince's servants had been named as the thief. The thief, he reasoned, had hidden the jewel in wet plaster at the factory where a cousin worked, so that it had gone out into the world inside one of six busts. The man who was now breaking them was searching for the bust that held the pearl, and Holmes counted on him to find it, one hammer at a time.

By careful inquiry among the shops, Holmes discovered where the remaining busts had been sold, and he guessed that the last of the six, in the house of Mr Josiah Brown at Chiswick, would soon be attacked. He therefore took Watson and Lestrade to the garden, and there the three men crouched in the dark shrubbery for hours, while the night grew colder and Lestrade grew more doubtful. Holmes alone remained patient, for he knew that the man they wanted could not afford to wait.

At last a shadowy figure climbed through the window, carried the bust into the garden and smashed it at his feet. Holmes and Lestrade leaped out and seized the wretched man, an Italian named Beppo, and in the wreckage lay a small black pearl, which Holmes lifted into the lamplight with the air of a conjuror. Lestrade, forgetting his doubts, burst into applause, and Holmes bowed as a man bows to an honest audience.

Hilton Soames, a tutor at St Luke's College, came to Holmes in great distress, for the long proofs of an important Greek examination had lain on his desk that afternoon, and someone had been through them. A key had been left in his door, a servant named Bannister had been in the room, and three students lived in the rooms above, each of whom had reasons to want the prize. Holmes, who could not resist a puzzle in a quiet place of learning, travelled to the college at once.

In the study Holmes found some curls of pencil wood and a small lump of black clay, which together told him that the visitor had copied the papers in great haste. He then called on the three students, who were all very different: Gilchrist, a fine athlete, Daulat Ras, a calm and clever young man from India, and Miles McLaren, a brilliant but lazy fellow. Each was polite and nervous, and Holmes, whose eyes missed nothing, studied the three rooms, the three faces and the old servant Bannister who stood trembling in the corner.

Holmes explained that the black clay had come from the shoes of a long-jump athlete, and that only one of the three students had been in the jumping pit that afternoon. Gilchrist, white-faced and honest at heart, confessed that he had given way to temptation and read the papers, and that old Bannister, who had once served his father, had tried in a clumsy way to protect him. He withdrew from the competition that very day, and Soames, who had expected a villain, found himself touched by the boy's open shame.

Inspector Stanley Hopkins came to Baker Street with a problem at Yoxley Old Place, where the secretary of the invalid Professor Coram, a young man named Willoughby Smith, had been found stabbed in the grounds. The dying man had spoken only a few words, and clutched in his hand were a pair of gold pince-nez, the sort of eyeglasses that grip the nose with a spring. They were a woman's, Holmes said at once, and from them he proceeded to tell Hopkins an astonishing number of things about their owner.

From the glasses alone, Holmes described their owner: a woman of good education and some means, with a narrow nose and eyes set close to it, so short-sighted that she could hardly walk without them. At Yoxley Old Place he studied the professor's rooms with the same quiet attention, and he noticed that the bedroom opened directly off the study, which meant that a person might have been hiding there while the housekeeper searched. Hopkins listened with growing respect, though he did not yet see where the reasoning led.

In the professor's own rooms, Holmes opened a hidden space and led out a tall, pale woman with failing eyes, who confessed that she had come to the house to find the professor, whom she knew by another name. They had been comrades in a movement against the Czar in Russia years before, she said, and he had betrayed his friends to save himself, with terrible results for those who trusted him. Smith had seized her in the dark, she had struck out in fear, and she had never meant him to die.

Cyril Overton, the huge captain of the Cambridge rugby team, rushed into Baker Street in despair, for his best three-quarter, Godfrey Staunton, had vanished from his hotel on the eve of the great match against Oxford. A late message had reached the young man, and after reading it he had slipped out into the night, leaving his companions to suppose that he would come back before long. Holmes, who confessed that he knew little about rugby, took the case because the disappearance had an air of mystery that interested him.

In Cambridge, the great physician Dr Leslie Armstrong coldly refused to answer any of Holmes's questions, and the detective, who disliked being checked, determined to learn his secrets by other means. He borrowed a hound named Pompey and, having smeared a few drops of aniseed on the wheel of the doctor's carriage, let the dog follow the trail along the road for many miles. At the end of it stood a lonely cottage, and in one window a small light burned.

In the cottage, Holmes found Godfrey Staunton in tears beside the bed of his young wife, the daughter of his landlady, whom he had married in secret and who lay dying of a lung illness. He had not dared to tell his uncle, Lord Mount-James, an old miser who held the family money, and Dr Armstrong had gently kept the secret, as a good doctor should. Holmes told the whole story to Overton, who had come in anger, and the captain forgave his friend at once.

Inspector Hopkins hurried Holmes down on a winter morning to the Abbey Grange in Kent, where Sir Eustace Brackenstall, a rich and violent drinker, had been found dead in his dining room. His young wife, Lady Brackenstall, told in a weak voice how three burglars had burst in at night, bound her to a chair with the bell-rope and struck down her husband with the poker. Hopkins thought that the tale pointed straight to the notorious Randall gang, for whom he had been looking for some time.

In the dining room, Holmes examined the bell-rope that the burglars were said to have torn down, and he saw at once that it had been cut, not pulled. The knots which bound the lady to her chair were a sailor's knots, he added, and the Randall gang would hardly have wasted time on such neat work. The inspector, who had been so sure of his theory, began to look at his own boots in discomfort.

Holmes followed his clues to a young sea captain named Jack Croker, who had known Lady Brackenstall since the days when she was a girl in Australia and who had loved her ever since. Croker, who was too honest to deny anything, admitted that he had gone to the house that night and that he, the lady and her maid had lied to the police. He told them that Sir Eustace, drunk and cruel, had struck his wife, and that in a moment of fury Croker had killed the man with the poker.

Holmes, after hearing Croker's confession, proposed that the company should act as a private court of justice, with himself as the jury, and he pronounced the captain not guilty. The man had defended a helpless woman against a drunken brute, he reasoned, and no purpose would be served by hanging him for it. The sailor and the lady, who had suffered enough, were left to find what happiness they could.

Lord Bellinger, the Prime Minister, and the Right Honourable Trelawney Hope, the European Secretary, came together to Baker Street, an honour that Holmes took calmly, and they begged him to find a stolen letter from a foreign ruler. It had been locked in a despatch box in Hope's own bedroom, and it had vanished in the few hours between dinner and morning, though no one had seen a thief. If its contents became known, the Prime Minister gravely told him, the result in Europe might be war within a week.

Holmes suspected that a clever foreign spy named Eduardo Lucas had a hand in the theft, but when he and Watson reached the house in Godolphin Street, they learned that Lucas had been found murdered in his sitting room. Inspector Lestrade, who was in charge of the case, took them to the room, where the dead man's blood had soaked through the carpet and made a great dark stain. Holmes, who disliked a crime that had come before he could prevent it, walked in without a word.

In the room where Lucas had died, Holmes knelt on the carpet and noticed that the great stain upon it was not exactly above the stain on the boards beneath. That proved that the carpet had been lifted and put back, and the police, who had guarded the house closely, had let no one in, yet someone had plainly come and gone again unseen. Holmes, with a glance at the floor and a little smile, said that the second stain was the best clue he had been given in many years.

Holmes lifted a loose board in the floor and drew out, from a hollow beneath it, the missing letter itself, where the dead spy had hidden it before his death. He then called upon Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, the wife of the European Secretary, who admitted in tears that she had taken the letter from her husband's despatch box in order to protect a foolish secret from her youth. Holmes, who had no wish to ruin a good woman for an old mistake, quietly promised to keep her out of the affair.

The Prime Minister and the European Secretary returned to Baker Street, anxious and pale, and Holmes asked Mr Hope to unlock the despatch box once more. There, among the papers, lay the foreign ruler's letter, as safe as when it had first been placed there, and the two statesmen stared at it as though it were a ghost. Holmes, with a courteous smile, declared that the matter was ended and that certain secrets must remain with the person who solved them, and so closed the last case of his return.
